newsitem.title: CANADA: CS shares lose ground as bid talk heats up.
newsitem.headline: CS shares lose ground as bid talk heats up.

text.p: Shares in takeover target CS Resources Ltd lost ground in busy volume on Monday after jumping last week on a planned takeover bid by Gulf Canada Resources Ltd.

But speculation remained hot on CS's statement after Gulf's bid announcement on Friday that the high-tech heavy oil producer would soon be in a position to reveal a strategic alliance with another firm.
CS shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange were down 0.20 to 14.80 on almost 1.1 million shares.
Gulf said on Friday it planned to make a C$413 million takeover bid for CS in a cash or stock deal.
Under the proposal, Gulf would offer CS shareholders either C$14.50 in cash, subjected to a maximum cash portion of C$100 million, or 1.1539 Gulf shares for each CS share.
CS officials have not returned calls since Friday, but analysts said the company could be close to finalizing the strategic alliance deal in attempts to thwart Gulf's advance.
Scott Inglis, analyst with FirstEnergy Capital Corp, said CS's announcement left the impression that the alternative deal would not be a takeover proposal.
Inglis said it appeared a deal would be structured in a way that would see another company trade heavy oil properties and perhaps some cash with CS in return for an equity stake in the company.
The firm most mentioned as a potential partner for CS was PanCanadian Petroleum Ltd, although a PanCanadian spokesman declined to comment if a deal was in the works.

"We are a company that is on a growth path and that presents many opportunities, but we don't talk about them or identify any of them at any time before they're ready," PanCanadian's Alan Boras said. "So we aren't talking about any deal that may or may not be in the works with CS."
Boras said PanCanadian decided this year to devote more of its exploration and development budget away from heavy oil and toward light oil, natural gas and international opportunities.
"It would be basically an about-face (for PanCanadian) if it turns out to be true from what they've been saying about the commodity," Inglis said.

The discount that exists for Canadian heavy oil compared to light oil has widened over the past year, leaving some players to believe the situation could worsen with billions of dollars directed in Canada to heavy oil projects.

He also said an alliance deal would need to be attractive enough to convince CS shareholders, who have lived with a lackluster stock market performance, that it would be better than selling out at C$14.25 or higher.
"Just because the strategic alliance option is there doesn't mean that someone else doesn't come in and make a bid for it," he said.

Other firms that have been speculated as potential suitors for CS include Alberta Energy Co Ltd and Canadian Natural Resources Ltd, both of which are developing heavy oil and have shown a preference for friendly acquisitions.
